terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō), with the dative; also written as two words, satis faciō
evidence: Cic. Att. 2.4.3: dē geōgraphiā dabō operam ut tibi satis faciam
terms.comment: To do enough for someone, to meet what he wants or expects (Lewis & Short). It also means to make amends, to apologise (alicui satisfacere after an offence), and to pay a creditor in full; the context tells which.

terms.grammar: adjective: with the ablative of the thing
evidence: Phaedr. 3.18.10–14: omnēsque propriīs sunt contentae dōtibus
terms.comment: “Satisfied with”: contentus suīs rēbus, content with what one has (Cic. Parad. 51, Lewis & Short). A different word from contentus, “strained”, the participle of contendō.

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, with the dative
terms.comment: Latin often turns “I’m satisfied with it” round: mihi placet, it pleases me.

evidence: Caes. BG 6.9: Ubiōrum satisfactiōnem accēpit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A false friend: classically an apology or explanation offered to someone, and after Augustus amends for an injury (Tac. Germ. 21), not the feeling of being satisfied (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: dē geōgraphiā dabō operam ut tibi satis faciam; sed nihil certī polliceor.
phrases.english: About the geography, I’ll do my best to satisfy you; but I promise nothing definite.

phrases.latin: tibi forma, vīrēs aquilae, lusciniō melos, augurium corvō, laeva cornīcī ōmina, omnēsque propriīs sunt contentae dōtibus.
phrases.english: to you beauty, to the eagle strength, to the nightingale song, to the raven augury, to the crow omens on the left, and all are content with their own gifts.

sources: Lewis & Short: satis (satisfacio) · Lewis & Short: contentus · Lewis & Short: placeo · Lewis & Short: satisfactio
